name: Breaking the Chain: The Fight to End Slavery
description: From the Atlantic trade to the Thirteenth Amendment: the rebels, writers and politicians who ended legal slavery, and the late endings that followed.

checkpoints.name: A trade in people
checkpoints.note: From the early sixteenth century ships carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, a trade in which firms such as the Royal African Company took part. The Quakers were among the first groups to condemn slavery and to refuse to own people.

checkpoints.name: Revolt and law
checkpoints.note: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose in 1791. Toussaint Louverture led the revolution until the French seized him in 1802, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent in 1804. In the United States the cotton gin made cotton farming more profitable and tied it more firmly to slavery. Britain passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833.

checkpoints.name: Voices of freedom
checkpoints.note: Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery, became a leading speaker and writer. Sojourner Truth spoke for abolition, and Harriet Tubman helped others flee north. Uncle Tom's Cabin reached a wide public in 1852, and John Brown's raid in 1859 pushed the country nearer to war.

checkpoints.name: War and amendments
checkpoints.note: After Abraham Lincoln's election the American Civil War began in 1861. His Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people in rebel areas free, and the Gettysburg Address spoke of the cause. The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery in 1865; the Fourteenth followed in 1868 in the Reconstruction era.

checkpoints.name: Late endings and memory
checkpoints.note: The Empire of Brazil ended slavery in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so, the year before the monarchy fell. The 1977 television miniseries Roots followed one family from Africa through slavery and brought the history before millions of viewers.
